title: Breakouts

inOneLine.simple: A breakout is when price moves out through a support or resistance zone. Decide in advance what counts as one.
inOneLine.balanced: Define a [[breakout]] with a written rule, for example "a candle closes at least 5 pips beyond the zone". Without a rule, every wick through a line looks like a breakout afterwards.

explain.simple: Price can poke through a level and come straight back. So people use rules. A common one is to wait for a candle to close beyond the zone, not just touch it with a wick. Some add a small extra distance, called a filter. The rule is your choice. What matters is that you write it down before you look, and use it the same way every time.
explain.balanced: A wick-only move outside the zone that closes back inside does not meet a close-based rule. A bigger filter means fewer breakouts are counted, but you enter later and further from the level, so a [[stop-loss]] on the other side of the zone is wider. A breakout can continue, stall, or fail. Many fail, which is why the next lesson is about [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]. Breakouts around news can come with [[slippage]] and wider [[spread|spreads]].

assumptions: Your written rule: a breakout is a close at least 5 pips above the top of the zone, so at or above 1.10550
steps: Candle A: high 1.10560, close 1.10470. The wick went above 1.10550, but the close is inside the zone. Not a breakout under this rule.
Candle B: close 1.10580. That is 1.10580 − 1.10500 = 8 pips above the zone, which is at least 5. This counts as a breakout.
If you bought at 1.10580 with a stop just below the zone at 1.10430, the stop distance would be 1.10580 − 1.10430 = 15 pips.
Counting it as a breakout says nothing about whether price will keep rising.

assumptions: Rule: a breakdown is a close at least 10 pips below the bottom of the zone, so at or below 149.70
steps: A candle closes at 149.75. That is 149.80 − 149.75 = 0.05 = 5 pips below the zone. Not enough under this rule.
The next candle closes at 149.62. That is 149.80 − 149.62 = 0.18 = 18 pips below. This counts.
With a 5-pip filter, the first candle would have counted. The rule you choose changes which moves you call breakouts.

explainSimpler: A breakout is price leaving the box. Decide before you look what "leaving" means, for example a close outside it.
commonMistake: Calling every wick through a line a breakout, or changing the rule after the fact so the chart fits. Another mistake is assuming a breakout will run far.

quickCheck.prompt: Resistance zone tops out at 1.25000. Your rule: a breakout is a close at least 5 pips above it. A candle has high 1.25080 and close 1.24980. Is it a breakout?

options.text: No: it closed back inside the zone
options.explanation: Right: only the wick went above. The close at 1.24980 is below 1.25000.

options.text: Yes: the high went 8 pips above the zone, past the 5-pip filter
options.explanation: No: your rule is about the close, not the wick. The close was below 1.25000.

quickCheck.prompt: You make your breakout filter bigger, from 5 to 15 pips. What usually changes?

options.text: Fewer moves count as breakouts, and entries are later
options.explanation: Right: a stricter rule waits for more distance, so it confirms less often and later.

options.text: False breakouts stop happening, because the filter screens them all out
options.explanation: No: a filter only changes which moves count. Some breakouts that pass it still fail.
No: the filter changes which candles meet the rule.

doItNow.instructions: Write a breakout rule in one sentence, for example "a close at least 5 pips beyond the zone". Then open the Breakout or fake? drill in Practice and apply that same rule to every chart.
